map_subtitle: 62-year-old Thai man with fresh haematemesis and black tarry stools starting 2 hours before arrival
case_title: Acute Upper GI Bleeding from Peptic Ulcer Disease — NSAID + H. pylori, Gastric Antral Ulcer (Forrest Ib)

patient.name: Mr. Wichai
patient.chief_complaint: Vomiting bright red blood and passing black tarry stools, starting 2 hours before arrival at hospital

dtp.rationale: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for two continuous weeks caused gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding — an adverse drug reaction that has already occurred. The patient had a valid indication and took the drug as prescribed, so the problem lies in safety, not in indication or adherence.

monitoring.regimen: Fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid → high-dose IV PPI (omeprazole 80 mg bolus → 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) → endoscopic haemostasis within 24 hours → 14-day H. pylori eradication

efficacy.target: No continuing fall; consistent with Hb 9–10 g/dL
No recurrence of fresh blood; stool returns to normal colour

Proton Pump Inhibitor — suppresses gastric acid secretion

Esophagogastroduodenoscopy — endoscopy of the upper digestive tract

Black, sticky, tar-like stool from blood digested in the gut
The distal part of the stomach, just before the duodenum
An intravenous fluid such as normal saline or Lactated Ringer's

sections.title: Resuscitation and early treatment goals
rows: Initial assessment and resuscitation — always come first when a patient presents with haematemesis or melena
Protect the airway to prevent aspiration of blood into the lungs
Isotonic crystalloid such as 0.9% saline or Lactated Ringer's, intravenously
Risk stratification is required to decide how urgently endoscopy is needed

sections.title: Risk Stratification
rows: Used to decide whether the patient needs intervention such as urgent endoscopy or transfusion · a GBS above 0 indicates risk and a need for medical management
Raised BUN, Hb < 13.0 g/dL (men), systolic BP < 110 mmHg, pulse ≥ 100 bpm, melena, syncope, hepatic or cardiac failure
BUN > 25 = 6 points · Hb < 10 g/dL = 6 points · SBP 90–99 = 2 points · pulse ≥ 100 = 1 point · melena = 1 point · syncope = 2 points
Spurting / oozing bleeding — high risk of rebleeding, requires immediate endoscopic haemostasis
Visible vessel / adherent clot / flat pigmented spot — risk falls in that order · Forrest Ia through IIa are the group requiring endoscopic haemostasis
Clean ulcer base — the lowest risk of rebleeding
Age ≥ 60 is a high-risk factor for both rebleeding and death

rows: Omeprazole or pantoprazole — the mainstay for non-variceal bleeding
8 mg/hour for 72 hours after successful endoscopic haemostasis
Double-dose oral PPI (for example 40 mg twice daily) may be considered in low-risk patients
For variceal bleeding only, not for peptic ulcer bleeding
Standard triple therapy: standard-dose PPI + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily by mouth
14 days, for the best eradication rate
The offending agent must be stopped immediately while bleeding is active

step_1_problem_list.question: From the history (S) and the examination and laboratory findings (O), identify this patient's problem list at the level of diagnosis

choices.text: Age 62 and a raised BUN are the principal problems
H. pylori infection
Haematemesis and melena constitute a complete problem list
Chronic knee pain is the first problem to address
Hypovolaemic shock (from blood loss)
Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease

step_1_problem_list.clinical_rationale: The most life-threatening problem is hypovolaemic shock (BP 90/60, HR 115), caused by acute UGIB. The underlying pathology is peptic ulcer disease related to ibuprofen use together with H. pylori infection (RUT positive).

feedback.correct: Correct — a good problem list runs from the most life-threatening condition down to its cause: shock → acute UGIB → NSAID-induced PUD → H. pylori infection
feedback.partial: Partly correct — review which options are "signs and symptoms" and which are "diagnoses" that belong on a problem list
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — haematemesis and melena are only symptoms and signs, not a statement of the problem at the level of diagnosis

step_2_drps.question: Analysing this patient's use of ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily, which drug therapy problem contributed directly to this admission?

choices.text: Effectiveness — the ibuprofen dose is too low to control the pain
Drug interaction — an interaction with the antacid the patient is taking
Adherence — the patient forgot doses, which caused the gastric ulcer
Unnecessary drug therapy — this drug was never needed at all
Indication — the patient is taking the drug without a clear medical indication
Safety — the patient has had an adverse drug reaction that led to the bleeding
Dosage too high — the dose exceeds the maximum daily dose of ibuprofen

step_2_drps.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which protects the gastrointestinal mucosa, and can therefore cause ulceration and bleeding. A dose of 1,200 mg/day is a normal dose, but the harm to the mucosa is not reduced in proportion to the analgesic benefit.

feedback.correct: Correct — this is a safety DTP: the patient had a genuine indication and took the correct dose, but suffered an adverse reaction severe enough to require admission
feedback.partial: Partly correct — reconsider whether the patient had an indication for the drug, and whether the dose was appropriate
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — the patient took the drug as prescribed and had an indication for it (knee pain), so the problem is not indication, dose or adherence

step_3_etiology.question: Which factors acted together (a synergistic effect) to produce the Forrest Ib ulcer in this patient?

choices.text: Renal impairment reduced acid excretion and caused the gastric ulcer
A coagulation defect indicated by a raised INR
Inhibition of COX enzymes by ibuprofen
Thrombocytopenia preventing the bleeding from stopping
Chronic alcohol use causing oesophageal varices
Direct damage to the gastric mucosa by H. pylori
Vitamin deficiency from an unbalanced diet

step_3_etiology.clinical_rationale: Both NSAIDs and H. pylori are major risk factors for peptic ulcer disease. NSAIDs weaken mucosal defence by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, while H. pylori drives inflammation until the ulcer erodes down to a blood vessel.

feedback.correct: Correct — two mechanisms working together: reduced mucosal protection, and increased mucosal damage
feedback.partial: Partly correct — this patient has more than one contributing factor, and they reinforce each other
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — check the patient's platelet count, INR and creatinine before choosing a mechanism

step_4_risk_factor.question: Which of this patient's features indicate a high risk of rebleeding or death according to the guideline criteria?

choices.text: Age 62 (≥ 60 years)
AST/ALT within the normal range
A mildly raised white cell count
Systolic BP 90 mmHg (shock)
A history of NSAID use
Burning epigastric pain
Heart rate 115 bpm (> 100)

step_4_risk_factor.clinical_rationale: The recognised high-risk criteria are age ≥ 60, the presence of shock (SBP < 100 mmHg, pulse > 100 bpm), and comorbidities or medications that carry bleeding risk.

feedback.correct: Correct — the factors that count under the criteria are age, shock, tachycardia and use of a drug that causes bleeding
feedback.partial: Partly correct — review the numerical thresholds for SBP and pulse used to define the risk groups
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — burning epigastric pain and a mildly raised white cell count are not among the criteria that predict rebleeding

step_5_severity.question: Given BUN 35, Hb 8.5, SBP 90, HR 115, melena and light-headedness, together with the endoscopy findings, which statements about severity are correct?

choices.text: Forrest Ib (active oozing) falls in the group requiring endoscopic haemostasis
Forrest IIa (non-bleeding visible vessel)
GBS = 0, so the patient can be managed as an outpatient
Glasgow-Blatchford Score = 18, placing the patient in the very high risk group
Rockall Score = 0, placing the patient in the low risk group
Forrest III (clean ulcer base), low risk of rebleeding
GBS = 5, placing the patient in the moderate risk group

step_5_severity.clinical_rationale: Calculating the GBS: BUN 35 (> 25) = 6, Hb 8.5 (< 10) = 6, SBP 90 = 2, HR 115 = 1, melena = 1, syncope = 2, giving a total of 18 — very high (any GBS above 0 warrants admission and urgent endoscopy). Forrest Ib is an actively oozing ulcer and is classed as high risk.

feedback.correct: Correct — the GBS and the Forrest class point the same way: a high-risk patient needing urgent treatment
feedback.partial: Partly correct — work the GBS out component by component from the scoring table in the reference
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — go back to the BUN, Hb, SBP, HR and the light-headedness, and compare them with the GBS scoring criteria

step_6_current_therapy.question: During this acute phase of severe bleeding, how will you manage the patient's ibuprofen?

choices.text: Switch to a different NSAID that is less irritating to the stomach, at the same dose
Reduce the dose to 200 mg once daily
Continue it, but add an oral acid-suppressing drug alongside
Stop the drug immediately
Plan to move to a non-NSAID analgesic in future
Hold it for 3 days, then restart once the bleeding has stopped
Continue it, but take it immediately after food with plenty of water
choices.fatal_message: Taking the drug after food reduces local irritation to some extent, but it does not prevent systemic prostaglandin inhibition, which is the mechanism that causes the ulcer. Continuing the drug during active bleeding prevented the ulcer from healing, the bleeding worsened, and the patient died.

step_6_current_therapy.clinical_rationale: The offending agent must be stopped immediately. Continuing it during active bleeding prevents the ulcer from healing and can worsen the bleeding to the point of death.

feedback.correct: Correct — stop the causative drug at once, and plan a safer alternative for the joint pain in the longer term
feedback.partial: Partly correct — managing the causative drug has to cover both the acute phase and the long-term plan
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — this drug is the cause of the ulcer and the bleeding; reducing the dose or changing how it is taken is not enough

step_7_new_therapy.question: Which drug is the first-line agent with the strongest evidence for bleeding peptic ulcer (non-variceal bleeding) in this patient?

choices.text: Oral liquid antacid 30 mL every 2 hours
IV vitamin K to correct coagulation
IV ranitidine 50 mg every 8 hours
Oral sucralfate suspension to coat the ulcer
IV octreotide infusion
IV tranexamic acid to help stop the bleeding
IV proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole or pantoprazole

step_7_new_therapy.clinical_rationale: IV PPIs are the most effective way to hold the gastric pH above 6 so that clot remains stable. Octreotide is used only for variceal bleeding.

feedback.correct: Correct — IV PPI is the mainstay of non-variceal bleeding
feedback.partial: Partly correct — consider which drug acts quickly and powerfully enough to hold pH above 6 during acute bleeding
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — distinguish the drugs used for variceal bleeding from those for non-variceal bleeding, and check the patient's INR

step_8_goal.question: What are the goals of therapy for the first 24 hours in this patient?

choices.text: Reducing the pain score to 0/10 is the first priority
Maintain haemoglobin in the 9–10 g/dL range
Return the BUN to normal within 24 hours
Haemodynamic stability — systolic BP ≥ 100 mmHg
Get the patient back onto ibuprofen as usual
Eradicate H. pylori completely within 24 hours
Achieve haemostasis at the ulcer

step_8_goal.clinical_rationale: The first goal is resuscitation to stabilise the vital signs. The haemoglobin target in severe bleeding is 9–10 g/dL. Eradication is a long-term goal, not a goal for the first 24 hours.

feedback.correct: Correct — the first 24 hours are about circulatory stability, reaching the haemoglobin target, and successful haemostasis
feedback.partial: Partly correct — separate the acute goals from the long-term ones
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — review the numerical targets for SBP and Hb in the resuscitation section of the reference

step_9_therapeutic_plan.question: Choose the PPI prescribing plan for this Forrest Ib ulcer after successful endoscopic haemostasis

choices.text: Pantoprazole 40 mg IV push twice daily
IV PPI for 24 hours, then switch straight to the oral form
Omeprazole 80 mg IV bolus once, then stop
Omeprazole 80 mg IV bolus immediately
Give the drug on demand whenever the patient has abdominal pain
Omeprazole 20 mg orally once daily
Followed by a continuous infusion of 8 mg/hour for 72 hours

step_9_therapeutic_plan.clinical_rationale: This is the standard high-dose PPI regimen for high-risk ulcers (Forrest I and IIa), given to prevent rebleeding during the first 72 hours, when the risk of rebleeding is highest.

feedback.correct: Correct — an 80 mg bolus followed by an 8 mg/hour infusion for a full 72 hours is the standard regimen for high-risk ulcers
feedback.partial: Partly correct — the standard regimen always has two parts: a loading dose and a continuous infusion
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — review the dose, route and duration of high-dose IV PPI in the reference

step_10_efficacy_monitoring.question: Which parameters must be monitored every 4–8 hours in the early phase to assess the bleeding?

choices.text: The appearance and colour of the stool, or blood from the NG tube
Vital signs (BP, HR)
Serum magnesium every 4–8 hours
Pain score and knee range of movement
Haematocrit (Hct)
A repeat urea breath test every day
Serum amylase

step_10_efficacy_monitoring.clinical_rationale: Close monitoring of the vital signs and haematocrit shows whether haemostasis and fluid replacement are working, while stool appearance and NG tube output show whether bleeding is continuing.

feedback.correct: Correct — monitor the circulation, the blood concentration, and the evidence of ongoing bleeding
feedback.partial: Partly correct — consider which parameters change quickly enough to catch rebleeding in time
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — the chosen parameters must reflect the bleeding directly, not joint pain or slow-turnaround tests

step_11_adr_monitoring.question: If the patient receives high-dose IV PPI continuously for 72 hours, which adverse effects are the most common and should be watched for?

choices.text: Acute kidney injury
Sudden hair loss
Headache
A severe rise in blood pressure
Diarrhoea
Hypoglycaemia
Palpitations and tremor

step_11_adr_monitoring.clinical_rationale: Headache and diarrhoea are the principal adverse effects reported with PPIs.

feedback.correct: Correct — these are the most commonly reported adverse effects of PPIs
feedback.partial: Partly correct — this drug class has more than one common adverse effect
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — review the "PPI — adverse effects" entry in the reference

step_12_patient_education.question: Which counselling points are the most critical to emphasise to the patient before discharge from this stage?

choices.text: Do not buy NSAID painkillers or pre-packed drug sets to take without consulting a doctor or pharmacist
Drink milk before every dose of painkiller
Chew food thoroughly
Take the acid-suppressing drug only when the stomach hurts
Teach the patient to recognise warning signs such as black stools or vomiting blood
Stop drinking alcohol completely
No follow-up appointment is needed once the symptoms have gone

step_12_patient_education.clinical_rationale: The main precipitating factors are NSAIDs and alcohol; if they are not stopped, life-threatening rebleeding will follow. The patient also needs to recognise the warning signs so they can return to hospital in time.

feedback.correct: Correct — remove both precipitating factors, and make sure the patient knows when to come back to hospital
feedback.partial: Partly correct — review the social history and medication history for the behaviours that need to change
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — the most critical advice has to address whatever could make the patient bleed again

step_13_future_plan.question: Once bleeding has been controlled and the vital signs are stable, what is the most important next plan?

choices.text: Eradication is unnecessary because the NSAID history alone explains the ulcer
Continue a PPI for life without any repeat testing
Seven days of eradication antibiotics is sufficient
Arrange a follow-up EGD in 6–8 weeks
Use standard triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, twice daily)
Recommend gastrectomy to prevent cancer
Start H. pylori eradication therapy for 14 days

step_13_future_plan.clinical_rationale: Eradicating H. pylori is central to reducing ulcer recurrence, and a gastric antral ulcer needs follow-up endoscopy to confirm healing and to screen for malignancy.

feedback.correct: Correct — complete the 14-day eradication course, then repeat endoscopy to confirm healing and screen for malignancy
feedback.partial: Partly correct — the long-term plan includes eradication, the right regimen, and endoscopic follow-up
feedback.incorrect: Not correct — review the regimen and duration of eradication therapy, and why a gastric ulcer needs repeat endoscopy

authoring_notes.subjective_summary: 62-year-old man taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for two weeks with no gastroprotection, on a background of known PUD and chronic alcohol use
authoring_notes.objective_summary: Acute UGIB from a Forrest Ib gastric antral ulcer with hypovolaemic shock from blood loss, and a positive RUT
authoring_notes.vitals_interpretation: BP 90/60 = hypotension; HR 115 = tachycardia; RR 22 = tachypnoea; Temp 36.5 and SpO₂ 96% normal — consistent with Class II–III hypovolaemic shock
authoring_notes.lab_interpretation: Hb 8.5 and Hct 26 = low; WBC 12,500 = high; platelets, Cr, INR and AST/ALT normal; BUN 35 raised by digestion of blood protein in the upper gut together with prerenal azotaemia
authoring_notes.negative_findings_significance: The absence of jaundice and ascites argues against variceal bleeding from cirrhosis; the absence of petechiae or ecchymoses argues against a coagulation disorder; the absence of guarding or rebound tenderness helps rule out perforation
authoring_notes.gbs_calculation: BUN 35 (> 25) = 6, Hb 8.5 (< 10) = 6, SBP 90 = 2, HR 115 = 1, melena = 1, syncope = 2 → total 18 points
authoring_notes.forrest_interpretation: Forrest Ib = active oozing = high risk of rebleeding; requires endoscopic haemostasis and 72 hours of high-dose IV PPI
authoring_notes.etiology: NSAIDs inhibit COX, reducing the prostaglandins that protect the mucosa, while H. pylori damages the mucosa directly — a synergistic effect
authoring_notes.plan_summary: (1) Fluid resuscitation to correct the shock (2) High-dose IV PPI, 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour infusion (3) Endoscopic haemostasis within 24 hours, given the high GBS and the Forrest Ib ulcer
sources: Thai clinical practice guideline for the management of upper gastrointestinal bleeding, 2014
2024 ACG Clinical Guideline: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori Infection
